It was still wrong, and the mutation round is what said so: a faithful reintroduction of the doubled prefix on import reads 'Warning: <path>: warning: ...' -- lowercase second prefix -- and the case-sensitive count walks straight past it. M4 in the throwaway harness passed when it had to fail.

What the attempts share is the mistake: each asserted a property of the string in front of me rather than of the defect. Attempt 1 assumed the prefix is adjacent to the message; attempt 2 assumed a second prefix would be capitalised like the first. Both assumptions came from reading the output of the CORRECT code, where the defect is invisible by construction.

What I would do differently, and did on the fourth step: write the mutation first. Running M4 against attempt 2 took one command and settled in seconds what two rounds of reading the passing output did not. The suite being green is what made attempt 2 look finished, and green is exactly what a hole looks like.

properties.hypothesis: The guard was placed after the statements that write, not before them. setJournalModeWal writes the database header, so a refusal placed below it arrives after ascend has already modified the file it is refusing to modify.
what_was_tried: First placement: after verifyPragmas. The read-only arm then failed with PragmaError: journal_mode is delete -- a foreign file is not WAL, a read-only open cannot switch it, and the pragma read-back refused before anything asked whose file it was.

Second placement: after the pragma block, still above verifyPragmas. The message was right on every arm, but the byte-identity assertion failed: setJournalModeWal had already rewritten the header, so the refusal arrived after the write.

Third placement: the first statement of the open, before setJournalModeWal. Read sqlite_master, which needs no pragma and no schema, so it speaks first on every path. All three arms refuse with the foreign message and the file is byte-identical afterwards.

evidence_text: asc-63v guard placement. The byte-identity assertion is what caught the second attempt -- every message assertion in the file passed at that point. A guard against writing to someone else file has to be measured by whether the file changed, not by whether the refusal said the right thing.
